Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between Gromov centrality and the Gromov distortion, an upper bound of the Gromov centroid's centrality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Gromov centrality effectively captures the triangle inequality excess in various networks, including those with weights and networks lacking a triangle inequality.

Researchers have successfully developed a new solution to the gravitational field equation of theory, which combines both gravity and the scalar theory, by utilizing the azimuthally symmetric gravitational field of a rotating body. This solution has numerous applications, one of which is its ability to explain the precession of the perihelion in the orbit of planets. Interestingly, this precession phenomenon can also be accounted for within the framework of the scalar theory. Furthermore, this new solution has potential implications for understanding the behavior of rotating black holes and black hole accretion disks.

Set theory's foundational role has been pivotal in mathematics, with its set-theoretic constructs serving as a framework for various mathematical theories. While this approach has been widely accepted, it has been criticized for its uniformity, prompting alternative foundations. One alternative is synthetic geometry, which has been explored by several scholars, including G. K. Wolf. This paper examines Wolf's concept of the synthetic ground field within the context of foundation theory. Drawing on recent research, the presentation offers a more general interpretation of Wolf's idea and explores potential applications to matrix theory, specifically the Jordan canonical form. Matrix pencils are considered as examples, highlighting possible advantages and limitations compared to ground field-based approaches.

We will establish that certain types of solvmanifolds qualify as $R$-exotic, taking into account the concept of topological T-duality and an isomorphism between solvmanifolds. Furthermore, our method can be applied to a broader category of manifold types beyond just solvmanifolds.

We've devised a new method to embed graphs of bounded genus and grid minor-free graphs into low-distortion grids, leveraging a recent breakthrough that reduced distortion grids to O(sqrt(log n)) for similar graph classes. This advancement allows us to improve upon previous approximation factors by an O(log n) term, and also results in a significant reduction of the grid's treewidth, from O(log^2 n) to O(log n) for minor-free graphs.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing understanding of their long-term behavior is already well-established. This study delves into discrete parabolic equations, focusing on the role of boundary conditions in determining the system's eventual behavior.

We investigate the simulation of the evolution operator in closed systems using variational quantum algorithms. Our study focuses on quantum and fermionic-excitation evolutions and compares them to established methods in the literature. By analyzing the effects of expressing the evolution operator as a sum of two terms involving qubit- and fermionic-excitations, combined with a quantum circuit ansatz, our findings reveal that qubit-excitations are more effective in achieving high-fidelity results with fewer measurements, particularly at short time intervals. Our research reveals that these unital Hamiltonians can be efficiently implemented using simple quantum circuits, making them suitable for near-term quantum devices. Our findings are further supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate the accuracy of the two-term sum approach in comparison to the standard sum of two-qubit terms. Our work paves the way for the development of novel hybrid quantum circuits that are well-suited to noisy quantum hardware.

Deep Generative Decoders (DGDs) are versatile image-to-image mapping systems that utilize deep generative models as their target output. In contrast to Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), DGDs circumvent the need for approximate optimization and relaxed relaxation conditions. VAEs, on the other hand, employ approximate Bayesian methods and rely on relaxation assumptions that involve approximate lower bounds. VAEs, however, introduce a significant bias in their loss function and relaxations, which are not present in DGDs. In this research, we investigate the bias inherent in VAEs and DGDs, and present a new, bias-free reconstruction loss function derived using Bayes' theorem. Our findings demonstrate that VAEs introduce an excessive, unnecessary reconstruction distortion, which is not present in DGDs or the proposed loss function. We also showcase the benefits of DGDs in generating high-quality reconstructions for image-to-image mapping tasks, using super-resolution as a case study.

The presence of a primordial stochastic gravitational wave background in our universe's current era could alter its expansion timeline. A thorough search for this phenomenon using data from Advanced LIGO's first observational period has yielded no detectable signal. Consequently, researchers have placed stringent limits on the amplitude of such phenomena across a range of frequencies, specifically between 25 Hz and 1 kHz. These limits have been used to place constraints on various cosmic inflation models, including those based on first-order phase transitions and a study of when this background likely emerged in our universe's history.

A spectral analysis of comets within the Solar System can reveal their chemical composition and movement patterns. Observations of the comet C/2015 ER61 using the APEX telescope have revealed its inner composition, which primarily consists of CO2, H2CO, NH3, SO, CS, SO2, HCN, N2H+, NO+, and OCS. These findings were compared with a dynamical model of the comet's nucleus, which allowed for a comprehensive understanding of its volatile emissions. The data also revealed a significant discrepancy between the comet's observed volatile emissions and its movement patterns, which can be attributed to a heterogeneous distribution of volatiles within the comet's nucleus.

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Our system relies on two readily available components: a self-supervised speech representation model and a large corpus of human transcribed speech. Notably, these components can be pre-trained using public datasets. Our method achieves comparable quality to traditional supervised neural synthesis techniques, with a notably lower overall requirement for labeled training data.

In this study, the behavior of the fractional energy density as a function of the equation of state parameter w is examined. A comparison with a fractal universe model reveals that the fractional energy density fails to describe a physically viable universe when w is 0.5 or greater. Furthermore, the model does not offer a viable dark energy solution. Our results indicate that the fractional energy density does not effectively extend our understanding of the universe's thermodynamic behavior.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems are challenging to find optimal solutions for in real-world applications. A new method called BnB-NSGAII combines multi-objective evolutionary algorithms with a branching and bounding technique to overcome this challenge. This paper evaluates the performance of BnB-NSGAII in comparison to a novel decomposition method called NOBLE in solving complex real-world problems. A custom-made test suite was created to facilitate this comparison, and extensive experiments were conducted to assess the performance of both approaches. A statistical analysis of the results showed that BnB-NOBLE outperformed BnB-NSGAII, achieving better quality solutions at a faster computation speed.

We establish an connection between two groupoids, demonstrating that they are linked by an internal groupoid over an algebraic structure, with one groupoid being subsumed by the other through this linking groupoid.
This relationship implies that classically defined Hausdorff Lie groupoids and their internal counterparts share the same level of path connectivity despite the internal groupoid lacking a smooth topology.
The result is achieved by employing a specific path space groupoid constructed using internal differential geometry methods developed in the context of sheaf-theoretic differential geometry.
These findings have the potential to be extended to cover more intricate scenarios, including path spaces on more intricate algebraic structures, as well as loop groups and action groupoids.

The Dynaswap project has developed a comprehensive security architecture for
cyberphysical systems, capable of detecting and neutralizing malicious input.
This innovative approach employs a sophisticated prediction system that can
identify and handle both anticipated and unanticipated legitimate user input,
while also providing real-time responses. Additionally, Dynaswap's
countermeasures can be seamlessly integrated into existing systems without
disrupting normal operations. To further enhance dynamic security, a predictive
model is regularly updated by monitoring system behavior both during and outside
of operational periods. A specific application of Dynaswap is showcased through
a case study on a cyberphysical system that manages a building's HVAC.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. This involves identifying the implicit emotions expressed towards specific aspects of the product. To achieve this goal, we developed a novel method called explicit-implicit sentiment disentanglement, which breaks down reviews into explicit and implicit emotions expressed about the product. Our approach utilizes disentanglement-based recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to model reviews and extract explicit and implicit emotions expressed about the product. To further enhance the model's performance, we incorporated a novel self-attention mechanism called Recurrent self-attention, allowing the model to focus on relevant words within the review. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art models in determining the sentiment of specific aspects.

We suggest an innovative method to evaluate linear mediation in binary situations within a stratified case-control framework. Stratified case-control studies are frequently employed in epidemiological research, allowing us to estimate odds ratios, which can be translated into log-linear relationships. We adapt a linear mediation approach to a group of models that can be used in both continuous and binary data settings, which includes a new strategy to deal with weights produced by sampling techniques in stratified case-control designs. We also present a method to determine confidence intervals for key metrics through the bootstrap technique. A simulation study is carried out to compare the effectiveness of our method against current methods used for sample size calculations in mediation analysis, which are designed for continuous data.

This research paper examines a wireless communication network with reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) that support both active and passive beamforming, with a focus on ensuring a minimum data rate for users. To address the challenge of few-shot continual learning, we propose a new approach called Executive Function-based Learning (Executive Functional Learning - EFL). By modeling executive functions as the ability to plan, control, and adapt to changing circumstances, we address the plasticity/stability dilemma inherent in this problem. In EFL, executive functions are used to determine when it's necessary to update existing knowledge and to identify relevant components of a previous model for adaptation to a new task. To reduce the computational complexity of this approach, we design a simplified version of the planning process that only considers the most likely beneficial paths. Furthermore, we introduce an online method for identifying the most relevant features and parameters in real-time. Experimental evaluations on continuous learning tasks with limited data demonstrate the effectiveness of EFL in achieving high performance and maintaining stable knowledge across multiple tasks.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) is poised to revolutionize our understanding of the solar wind's origins by making close approaches to the Sun. Researchers have used 2021 near-orbit data from Wide Field Survey Imager images to calculate the average solar wind energy flux, normalized to one solar radius, as 1.12±0.07 kW/m^2 K/s. This new metric provides a more relevant perspective than the traditional Kelvin temperature scale. By comparing this value to coronal mass ejection and fast solar wind data, scientists found that the energy in these phenomena is comparable to the solar wind's energy at a certain distance from the Sun's center. This discovery suggests that the solar wind's origin may be more complex than previously thought.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we have developed a framework for defining and studying noncommutative group cohomology. This involves creating a generalization of locally trivial G-C*-algebras and demonstrating that such structures can be represented as G-equivariant continuous fields of AF-algebras. Additionally, we have identified cohomological criteria that allow us to characterize noncommutative principal bundles and noncommutative affine Grassmannians. These findings are further illustrated through the examination of locally compact quantum groups, particularly in relation to their Haar cohomology, showing that infinite dimensional quantum groups always have positive Haar cohomology groups.

We demonstrate the existence of P-maximal families, including P-adherent families and families related to interiterable forcing of uncountable cardinals, as well as their counterparts in NEX models. Furthermore, we develop methods to construct these P-maximal object families in models of the Axiom of Determinacy.

In this research, several key aspects of optomechanical systems are examined from a theoretical standpoint, focusing on the occurrence of phase transitions. The influence of q-deformation on the linear stability analysis, the emergence of complex eigenvalues, and the associated phase transitions is specifically investigated. The findings indicate that q-deformation can lead to both type I and type II transitions, with the possibility of observing a third critical point in the context of a three-body system. Furthermore, the study explores the effect of q-deformation on the ground state energy. Additionally, the research considers a nonlinear analysis that reveals a nonlinear phase transition in the system, which can be identified by a second-order Hopf bifurcation.

In a One-Rotator Model, we've established that a two-class body exhibits the characteristic of R-negative scissors states. This model extension to a more intricate Two-Rotators Model has been explored, and our findings indicate that the emergence of R-negative scissors modes is contingent upon the presence of quadrupole deformation, and specifically, that only well-deficient oblate shapes exhibit this phenomenon.

A new method utilizing cell-averages and a neural network is designed to solve the Burgers equation, an example of a hyperbolic conservation law. By combining this neural network approach with a spatial discretization that calculates cell averages, the method can efficiently find a global solution, avoiding potential numerical issues. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional numerical approaches, particularly in terms of time step independence.

The ALICE experiment has been equipped with upgraded detectors, including a precise tracking system and an innovative vertex detector, to study heavy-flavor production and low-mass dielectron production with greater accuracy. A new artificial intelligence-based method has been developed to enhance the accuracy of reconstructing the trajectories of charged particles within the ALICE experiment's upgraded tracking detectors. This method, which involves a convolutional neural network, was tested on real data and showed significant improvements in track reconstruction efficiency, while maintaining low false-positive rates. The results indicate that this method can effectively recover lost tracks and reject spurious tracks. The track-finding algorithm was further refined by adding physics-based constraints, which allowed it to determine the trajectories of particles. These results have the potential to contribute to the ALICE experiment's ongoing research, including the investigation of properties of particles produced in high-energy collisions.

The Unruh effect, a well-established phenomenon, reveals that an observer undergoing constant acceleration perceives the vacuum as a thermal bath. Conversely, there's been limited understanding of the implications of perceiving the vacuum state as a result of time-varying acceleration. In this study, we explore the time-dependent case and find that the vacuum remains an invariant state, perceptible to accelerated observers through a specific signal. A quantum mechanical framework is employed to analyze this signal, revealing its resemblance to the dynamical Casimir effect. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the signal emitted by the accelerating observer can serve as a potential method to experimentally detect the time-dependent Unruh effect.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves discovering event occurrences along with their key components, which has been an area of active research in Natural Language Processing. This study introduces a novel unsupervised and domain-independent Event Extraction strategy that relies solely on annotated text data. According to this method, any word or phrase identified as part of an event is assigned the label 'event trigger,' which is then used to group dependent words and phrases into specific event patterns. This process enables us to recognize and categorize various event types along with their associated arguments, which are then used to compare and annotate different data sets. This unsupervised and domain-independent event extraction method has been tested on the SemEval-2010.4 dataset, where it achieved promising results, with F1 scores of 60.3% for event extraction, 57.1% for argument labeling, and 51.1% for relation detection, indicating that this technique can effectively identify and categorize various event types in a wide range of domains without prior training or supervision.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and a generated metric connection in its differential geometry. A key result is that an explicitly defined differential form, denoted $I$, is shown to be exact. Furthermore, an original proof is provided that an arbitrary power of $I$ can be represented as an exact differential form.

The X-ray emissions from high mass X-ray binaries in supergiant X-ray binaries are influenced by the presence of a stellar wind, which is captured by the compact object. Our research involves analyzing X-ray light curves from Cygnus X-1, observed by the Swift X-ray Telescope, to determine the impact of the stellar wind on X-ray variability. By comparing the power spectral density of the X-ray light curves from phases 0.4-0.6 and 0.9-1.0, we found that the lower wind-interactive phase has a higher power in low frequencies but a lower power in high frequencies. This indicates that the stellar wind has a minimal effect on X-ray emissions at phase 0.9. However, our analysis suggests that the X-ray emissions from Cygnus X-1 are characterized by a low Q factor, which is consistent with the concept of a red noise spectrum.

The introduction of a non-abelian aether-like term in the action of a quantum field theory leads to significant changes in power counting renormalizability. A renormalizable $R^2$ gravity theory can be obtained by coupling this term to the field strength tensor of a massless spin-1 field. Our analysis demonstrates that this gravitational theory remains renormalizable to a one-loop order by applying a combination of a non-local curvature contraction and the addition of specific counterterms and massless spin-1 fields in the loop expansion of the gravitational theory.

We investigated the feasibility of simultaneously modeling syntax and semantics. To do this, we developed a system that creates a unified syntactic-semantic representation by parsing sentences with a pre-trained neural model. We experimented with different systems, including one that takes into account the context of the text, and another that uses a pre-trained model to capture the relationships between the words in the sentence. We found that our approach outperforms existing systems on several benchmarks, including one that measures the accuracy of the syntax and another that measures the accuracy of the semantics. We also found that our approach generalizes well to sentences that are longer than 20 words.

The relationship between the angular momentum of black holes and the mass ejected during the merger of black holes is examined through a set of simulations. These simulations involve black holes with masses ranging from 10 to 100 solar masses and spins as high as 0.9. It is discovered that the mass ejected during the merger is significantly influenced by the angle at which the black holes approach each other. When the angle of approach is close to 90 degrees, the amount of mass ejected is at its maximum. By using a specific formula, the amount of mass ejected can be estimated for any given system. Furthermore, the frequency of high-energy bursts produced by the ejected mass is estimated, and the results suggest that such bursts could potentially be detected by the Advanced Atacama Large Millimeter Array.

A thorough investigation of tidal features in massive early-type galaxies was conducted using Hubble Space Telescope data in the Virgo cluster. Out of 177 massive early-type galaxies, a significant portion (26%) exhibited distinct tidal features with high flux fractions, and an analysis of their spatial distribution and morphology provided insights into their formation. It was found that tidal features are more prevalent in less luminous and lower mass galaxies, and their prevalence decreases with increasing stellar mass. A comparison with other studies revealed that tidal features are more common in the inner regions of the Virgo cluster than in the Coma cluster, and a relationship between tidal features and substructure was observed. A low-density environment was found to favor tidal feature formation, and it is hypothesized that tidal features may result from tidal interactions between galaxies and dark matter.

Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation offers a novel gravitational model
characterized by an asymmetric, repulsive force that mimics the effects of
centrifugal gravity. This model suggests that a gravitational anomaly, akin to
dark energy, is a manifestation of repulsive gravity, occurring near the poles
of rotating gravitating bodies. Given its focus on axisymmetric systems, this
model is particularly well-suited for explaining the properties of rotating
neutron stars. Introducing a modification to Einstein's General Relativity,
Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation includes a new constant that
determines the strength of repulsive gravity, resulting in altered equations
for hydrostatic equilibrium and mass distribution in such systems.

Recent breakthroughs in detecting repeating fast radio bursts (FRBs) have generated significant interest in their origins. Researchers have proposed that optical counterparts to FRBs could be produced by neutron star mergers or by magnetars in galaxy nuclei. We present an in-depth examination of these magnetar models, specifically examining how the optical and radio waveforms are linked. We estimate the likelihood of detecting optical counterparts to FRBs using data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, the Advanced Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope system, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We have calculated the implications of these findings for actual observations, specifically for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We have established that approximately 100 flare events could be detected by the Rubin Observatory within a specific time frame, and that approximately 10 of these events could be detected optically. We have also established that approximately one flare event could be detected optically every 10 years.
