The study examines various oversampling techniques, such as SMOTE, to rectify class imbalance issues in classification tasks. A novel approach called Linear Nearest Neighbour Over Sampling is introduced, featuring a linear method to synthesize new minority class samples. Performance of LNNOS and SMOTE is compared using comprehensive experiments on datasets with differing degrees of imbalance, showing LNNOS to outperform SMOTE on imbalanced datasets, although falling slightly behind on balanced ones. The inclusion of LNNOS in existing oversampling techniques, such as LNNOS with Adaptive Boosting and LNNOS with Adaptive Boosting using LOTS, is proposed, revealing enhanced performance, specifically with the combination of Adaptive Boosting.

This study examines the connection between COVID-19 coverage in local news and public health outcomes. By analyzing nearly 100,000 news articles from over 1,000 local outlets, we discovered a time-varying correlation between mentioning national COVID-19 death rates and local disease prevalence. We also found that local news often reinforced fear-inducing content, but rarely offered coping strategies, which may have contributed to negative mental health effects among readers. By mapping news dissemination, we observed that areas with high social inequality and lower health resilience were more susceptible to COVID-19 coverage that could exacerbate public health risks. These findings highlight local news outlets' responsibility to consider the long-term public health and societal impacts of their content choices.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) has the potential to accurately simulate astrophysical fluid dynamics, but only if its mass, momentum, energy, and angular momentum conservation properties are properly maintained. Recent breakthroughs in this field have allowed for the development of higher-order conservative SPH schemes, which can now guarantee these fundamental conservation laws. A comprehensive review of these developments is provided, along with an in-depth analysis of two novel approaches: a local pressure and internal energy conservative scheme, and a higher-order artificial viscosity method.

The ratio of Sachs electric to magnetic form factors, represented as $G_E/G_M$, is 
crucial in determining the degree of longitudinal polarization transfer during an 
interaction, with this ratio varying significantly across different experiments. 
A recent investigation by the Rec-E15-8 experiment at JLab has sought to resolve this 
discrepancy by analyzing data within the range of 2 to 6.0 GeV. Utilizing an advanced, 
high-resolution detector, researchers employed a precise electron beam polarized in 
the plane and utilized $^{12}$C targets to conduct their analysis. Utilizing novel 
kinematic reconstruction techniques, scientists were able to achieve unprecedented 
accuracy in measuring the polarization of the recoil proton, with an estimated error of 
approximately 10%. Utilizing these precise measurements, scientists were able to 
determine the ratio of $G_E/G_M$ with unprecedented accuracy, with measured values of 
approximately 0.78 and 0.84 at $Q^2$ values of 4 and 6 $GeV^2$, respectively. 
These results indicate a $Q^2$ dependence that is consistent with magnetic and electric 
magnetic form factors having the same functional form, with an estimated magnetic 
magnetic form factor of approximately $0.85(Q^2/0.6)^{\eta}$, with $\eta$ varying from 
0.15 to 0.25.

We introduce a novel method for leveraging artificial states in data-efficient learning through reinforcement and imitation learning. Our proposed approach involves constructing a set of hypothetical states based on assumed system dynamics, and using these virtual states to gather synthetic experience. By applying supervised and reinforcement learning algorithms within this synthetic experience framework, our method achieves a notable reduction in real-world data requirements for both reinforcement and imitation learning tasks. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in facilitating learning with minimal data in a cartpole environment.

A comprehensive search for the production of two Higgs bosons simultaneously or a Higgs boson paired with a heavy photon is carried out using LHC collision data. This analysis utilizes datasets from the ATLAS and CMS experiments, encompassing 139 fb^-1 of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions in 2015 and 2016. Six separate searches are conducted to identify signs of new physics, including non-resonant and resonant Higgs boson pair production, as well as a Higgs boson paired with a heavy photon. No significant signals are observed in the data, leading to stringent constraints on both the phenomena and potential new physics. Specifically, upper limits on the cross-section of non-resonant Higgs boson pair production are set, consistent with predictions from the Standard Model. Additionally, upper limits on the cross-section of resonant Higgs boson pair production are set, placing stringent constraints on inert doublet models. It is also determined that the production cross-section of a Higgs boson paired with a heavy photon is limited, with implications for leptoquark models.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating techniques combine high sensitivity, extensive dynamic range, and rapid response times. Despite these advantages, their full potential as reliable, long-term stable devices has not been realized due to ongoing nonlinear self-oscillations. We have developed a method to stabilize the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations using feedback control, achieving long-term stability of 10^-4 Hz over a period of 24 hours. This method is compatible with existing magnetometer designs and does not compromise their existing capabilities.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls within the range of $0 \leq \rho(X) \leq 10$. Focusing on the extreme cases of $\rho(X)=0$ and $\rho(X)=10$, this research provides a method to construct such K3 surfaces utilizing the theory of integrable systems, a theory that also allows for classifying relevant extreme K3 surfaces based on their symplectic automorphism order.

In a supergravity unified framework with spontaneous R-parity violation, neutralino dark matter is proposed for minimal models with sequential tribimaximal and theoretical A4 symmetry. This theoretical framework, which incorporates standard model fermions and gauge bosons, is then analyzed for neutralino dark matter. Furthermore, a new superpotential, which breaks R-parity through spontaneous symmetry violation, is presented for the minimal supergravity unified model of type-I. This model, which features three families of standard model multiplets, has three sequential tribimaximal neutrino mass matrices and three theoretical A4 symmetry.

The main idea behind our research is to develop an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (EPTAS) for finding maximum independent sets in planar and bipartite graphs with a bounded genus value. This achievement is achieved by leveraging a novel classification method for sparse structures, specifically applied to the fractional chromatic number. This classification, along with a new Integer Programming formulation that has a linear number of variables and constraints, enables our algorithm to efficiently handle most cases where exact solutions can be found in Polynomial Time. This study represents the first known result demonstrating that maximum independent set can be exactly solved in non-NP-hard cases for planar and bipartite graphs. Furthermore, our research also extends to minimum vertex cover problems on these graph types.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly reducing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance guarantees are established for both homogeneous and heterogeneous data environments, supported by experiments demonstrating the benefits of the method and its performance comparisons with existing algorithms.

This paper presents a study on detecting hate speech in Hindi and Bengali through transfer learning from English models. We utilize a Transformer-based architecture, Punctuated BERT, to investigate the transferability of hate speech detection models across languages. The results reveal that English models can effectively generalize to punctuated Bengali and Hindi texts. Furthermore, we leverage a large multilingual corpus, X-RoL101L, to enhance the performance of hate speech detection in low-resource languages by fine-tuning models on this extensive training dataset. The findings demonstrate the potential for transfer learning to improve hate speech detection in resources-constrained languages.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to distinguish the direction of nuclear recoils is crucial, especially for investigating dark matter particles at low energies, high-energy neutrinos generated by the sun and ice cube, and specific nuclear physics reactions. A new technique using a laser to detect nuclear recoils in solid argon is being developed, building on past experiments with liquid argon that successfully used a similar method to detect electron recoils. By demonstrating this new technique with a small sample of solid argon, we have achieved a key breakthrough, namely creating nuclear recoils using MeV-range protons and then using a laser to detect them. A dark matter search, however, will require much larger argon volumes, lower proton energies, and highly sensitive equipment.

A comprehensive understanding of commercial driving behavior is crucial for improving road safety. We introduce a data-driven approach for behavioral analysis, which incorporates contextual factors beyond the driver's immediate control. We expand the existing driving dataset with additional data points to account for these external influences and propose an advanced data collection method to enrich the existing information. We apply our approach to real-world data from the SmartCity project in Helsinki, Finland, to illustrate its effectiveness and effectiveness in considering contextual factors affecting driving behavior.

This paper presents a groundbreaking study on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) in natural scenes, demonstrating the limitations of current OCR models due to insufficient generalization capabilities. The existing models rely heavily on a perfect pipeline, comprised of text detection, OCR, and Knowledge Graph Construction, which fails to address real-world applications. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel end-to-end OCR scene recognition model, SceneOCR, capable of handling text detection and recognition seamlessly. Furthermore, we introduce a novel training strategy, Curriculum Learning, to enhance the model's performance. The proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art on various benchmarks, including Wild-text, ABYWild, and AITech, with improvements of 4.9, 4.0, and 3.0 points in F-score, 5.3, 5.3, and 5.0 points in Recall, and 4.9, 4.6, and 4.3 points in Precision, respectively.

Random fields in various disciplines are represented as random functions with multivariate normal distributions, which include spatial and temporal processes as well as other types of random fields. Fitting these models to random data involves a complex optimization problem that is often infeasible to solve directly due to its high computational cost. A notable exception is a class of hyperparameter estimators based on restricted maximum likelihood, known as REML estimators, but even they struggle with large datasets. A notable solution is the inclusion empirical Bayes method, which offers significant advantages in terms of model accuracy and computational efficiency. By combining this method with the Randomized Coordinate Ascent REML (RCAR) algorithm, researchers can fit a broad class of Gaussian models in a reasonable time. A comprehensive numerical study demonstrates the efficacy of this method in a wide range of applications.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For L-functions associated to newforms with coefficients in a finite extension of the rational numbers, and under a specific condition regarding the coefficients' complexity, we show that when evaluated at critical points of the L-function, the bounding of its algebraic component in the denominators confirms the Riemann Hypothesis for automorphic L-functions over these fields, as initially proposed by the authors.

In a study, researchers investigated the electronic properties of armchair graphene nanoribbons with a specific width of 6 Angstroms using a tight-binding model. The model considered only nearest-neighbor hopping and accounted for different types of deformations: zigzag, sawtooth, and random. The findings showed that in a system with a large band gap, all types of deformations induce a significant spin polarization, which increases with band gap size. The random deformation pattern produced a slightly lower spin polarization compared to the other patterns but still showed a significant effect. The researchers also discovered that in a system with no band gap, all types of deformations fail to induce a significant spin polarization. The study demonstrates that in graphene nanoribbons with a specific width, in a system with a band gap, all types of deformations can be used to induce a significant spin polarization, which can be an important consideration for the development of spintronic devices.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by a variety of examples for illustrative purposes.

Bang-Joon Lee and Sunyoung Kim previously demonstrated in 2016 that a Hamiltonian graph with an even number of vertices can be classified as pancyclic under specific degree conditions in its central half. This research extends their finding to the case of edge-pancyclic graphs, utilizing degree conditions in its central third, specifically, the 1/3 to 1/3 range.

The origin of the directed flow created by light particles in relativistic heavy-ion collisions remains unclear. This study investigates how different types of cross-sections for nucleon-nucleon collisions, particularly in the type of collisions involving p+A systems, impact the directed flow produced by $\pi$ and $\phi$ in such collisions. The directed flow is examined using two different collision models: the Monte Carlo Geometric Binaries + Background model and the Relativistic Hydrodynamics model. The cross-sections of various nucleon-nucleon collisions are evaluated using data from fixed-target experiments, while accounting for different types of nucleon-nucleon interactions. The results show that both types of collisions, BHBS+BX and RHQ, can reproduce the magnitude and slope of the directed flow measured in p+A collisions. However, considering the uncertainty in the cross-sections used, it is challenging to draw a clear conclusion about the specific type of cross-section that contributes most to the directed flow produced by $\pi$ and $\phi$.

The adaptive spectral-Kolmogorov-Arnold transform (ASK) method, a novel technique for multi-dimensional systems, is analyzed in this research. It employs a sparse-grid-based approach and demonstrates several key benefits over traditional time integration methods, particularly in terms of memory requirements and computational efficiency. As demonstrated through numerical examples, this method can achieve significant savings in terms of memory and CPU time, and these results are in line with expected trends.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history, focusing on the theory of complex resonances. Key points include a method for calculating resonance parameters, their role in scattering cross sections, and the concepts of R-matrix and phase shift. Additionally, I will discuss a novel approach to determining resonances in experiments, the most common of which are time-of-flight and scattering radius.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is a popular solution for the Schrödinger problem, solution constraints ensure a unique, non-degenerate outcome when marginal probabilities are strictly positive. However, non-stochastic or boundary-margin cases can result in degeneracy. This paper offers a comprehensive analysis of these degeneracy conditions and proposes a solution. A dual formulation is derived and implemented via the Sinkhorn algorithm, which provides a characterization of non-degeneracy. Ultimately, this approach enables the algorithm to converge for a broader range of marginal probabilities than previously established in literature.

The ATLAS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider recorded data from inelastic proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV during 2011. Using the complete data set, the inclusive production cross-section for top-quark pairs was determined in direct proton-proton collisions. Top-quark events were identified in the data by requiring at least one isolated, high-energy electron or muon, and a substantial amount of hadronic energy. After correcting for detector effects and background interference, the top-quark pair production cross-section was calculated by comparing observed data with Monte Carlo simulations of standard model proton-proton interactions. The results of this analysis are in agreement with theoretical predictions generated using fixed-order calculations and parton-shower resummation, with a measured production cross-section of 674 ± 14 (statistical) ± 12 (systematic) pb.

In a many-body localized system, the central degree of freedom's dynamics are studied when it's connected to a disordered array of two-level systems with 'N' components, all interacting through a 'J' coupling. Our findings indicate that this setup exhibits a two-stage process where the central degree of freedom's behavior is characterized by initial rapid fluctuations, slow decay, and a transient quasi-stationary phase, before eventually relaxing. This study provides a theoretical framework for understanding how to achieve and measure this quasi-stationary phase in experiments involving quantum systems.

This paper aims to determine under what conditions the generalized Bessel functions $B_{p, \alpha}(z)$ and $J_{p, \alpha}(z)$ will meet specific criteria for subordination to linear mappings in the unit disk, thereby establishing their starlikeness and convexity in the unit disk.

Urban settings provide unique opportunities for meaningful human connections to drive economic growth and innovation. However, current urban planning strategies often fall short in addressing the needs of "weak ties", which are crucial for fostering new relationships. As a result, cities may unintentionally limit the potential for physical and social interactions that are essential for improving productivity and adaptability. To better understand these dynamics, researchers have developed a new framework called the "Urban Connection Index" (UCI), which uses data on business success, network formation, and physical design to assess a city's capacity to support strong and weak ties. By applying this framework, researchers can gain valuable insights into the urban conditions that support or hinder the potential for new relationship formation, ultimately guiding urban design and policy decisions.

A novel nonlinear field-split preconditioner is introduced to efficiently solve complex two-phase flow and transport issues. This innovative method builds upon a previously developed four-field-split scheme and applies a two-step process to significantly reduce the computational complexity. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the system of equations resulting from the two-step process can be resolved using an iterative algorithm with a complexity that is comparable to that of a single equation from a more comprehensive four-field-split scheme. Furthermore, the proposed method is effectively integrated into a comprehensive two-phase flow and transport solver, utilizing a combination of fractional step approach, GMRES for non-linear iterations and a block diagonal based BiCGStab(l) with ILU factorization for linear systems.

The unique interaction between chiral molecules and specific polarized light makes enantiomers distinguishable. However, achieving a significant difference in interaction with left and right circularly polarized light is complicated by the identical interaction strength with molecules. Chiral dielectric rings can amplify this interaction difference through the coupling of electromagnetic modes. By using a specific ring geometry, the difference in interaction strength with left and right circularly polarized light can be significantly increased. This effect is further amplified when the ring is in a specific geometric configuration, resulting in much stronger interaction differences than previously possible.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, two-dimensional string theory, and the Breitenlohner-Keefe-Maison black hole metric. We first explore the CW d-closed structure of the CW d-operator and its role in two-dimensional string theory and Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, emphasizing boundary terms. We then demonstrate that the boundary terms in the actions and amplitudes of the theories are related to the CW d-operator. Furthermore, we compute the boundary variation of the actions and amplitudes, showing that these variations are related to the CW d-operator, confirming the consistency of these theories. We also discuss the implications of our findings for semi-classical black hole information loss and the information paradox.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve faster-than-light velocities. This research examines the Alcubierre metric as a solution to Einstein's equations, focusing on the required non-baryonic matter for propulsion. Key aspects of this work involve space distortion within the horizon of Einstein's spherical symmetry and space-time manipulation for transporting the warp drive. We explore a novel approach using both spherical symmetry and the Alcubierre metric, combining their features to create a new warp field. This new field allows us to investigate a symmetric warp drive generated by a point-like object within the horizon, utilizing a non-soliton field solution. Our findings reveal that substantial energy requirements for propulsion increase significantly when applying the shift vector $v_0$ to transport an object within the horizon, shifting from a linear relationship ($4\pi v_0^2$) in three-dimensional space to a quadratic relationship ($\pi R^2 + \pi r^2 + 2\pi rR$) for warp drive transportation.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure faces increasing pressure from population growth and rising demand, predicting its remaining service life becomes crucial for its effective management. However, this endeavor is complicated by the vast array of factors involved, such as underground conditions, material properties, and usage patterns. To address this challenge, this research proposes a novel method for categorizing underground assets based on their functional roles. By applying this approach, managers can focus on the most critical infrastructure components, thereby improving their decision-making processes. The proposed method relies on applying data mining techniques to a knowledge graph representing underground utilities, thereby classifying their functional roles. The results of our experiments indicate that this approach is capable of achieving high levels of accuracy in predicting underground asset ages.

In a linear combination of two-dimensional harmonic oscillator eigenstates, we analyze a Coulomb interaction system, where ions in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal undergo spin dephasing. We derive an analytical solution for spin dephasing in this setup, demonstrating that it depends on temperature, ion number, intermixing angle of ion internal spin orientations, and confinement geometry. Additionally, we examine the influence of varying harmonic oscillator eigenstate amplitudes on spin dephasing within the Wigner crystal.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces at a highly localized level.
It enhances signals using a tip and is highly sensitive to both the tip's shape
and the surface being examined. In this study, we used computational methods to
compare the TERS response of two types of spheres, metallic and dielectric.
Our analysis considered the effect of light interaction with the tip and target,
as well as the materials involved. We used simulations to model the tip and
dielectric sphere interaction with various shapes, sizes, and orientations.
Our results show that the enhanced scattering signal is a combination of two
effects: when the tip and dielectric interact with light and when the metal surface
itself scatters light. We used our model to predict optimal conditions for the
enhanced scattering signal, including specific distances between the tip and
dielectric sphere. Our study provides valuable insights for optimizing TERS
techniques involving metallic tips and dielectric spheres.

A phenomenon known as Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) is widely presumed to be produced by spinning dust. It is now possible to simulate this emission using a combination of numerical models and a radiation transfer code to analyze the emission in various galactic environments. A simulated AME map of the Milky Way is created using the M33 model for the galactic dust distribution and a code called SKYDUST to calculate frequencies. The resulting simulated map is then compared to actual observations from ALFAMA and ATILAS to assess its accuracy. A significant difference is observed between the simulated and observed AME intensity, particularly at higher latitudes. This discrepancy is attributed to the use of a single dust model, suggesting the need for multiple models to accurately represent galactic environments. It is also proposed that AME and dust emission may originate from different locations in the galaxy.

Ammonium sulfate, a salt composed of protons and polyatomic anions, can be viewed as a protonic ice mixture. Its phase diagram is complex, consisting of multiple crystal structures and transitions, some of which involve changes in proton arrangement. Recent studies using advanced computational methods have revealed that the phase diagram of ammonium sulfate is similar in some ways to that of water. Our first-principles simulations show that the monoclinic structure is the stable crystal form at room temperature, and that the phase transitions between different crystal structures are connected to significant changes in polymeric bond length. Additionally, we found evidence of two protonic transitions within ammonium sulfate, one of which matches the monotropic transition observed experimentally. Our results suggest that the monotropic transition observed in ammonium sulfate is primarily a result of the reorganization of protons rather than changes in crystal lattice structure.

In probabilistic learning, organisms often struggle to decide between two choices with uncertain outcomes.  Many studies have found that many species, including humans, tend to follow a strategy that maximizes the chances of success by sticking with what worked before, rather than exploring the other option.  This "sticking with what worked" is called probability-matching and is seen as a sign of learning.  However, our research shows that this strategy can also be explained by a different process - one that actively avoids the wrong answer by ignoring unreliable information.  This alternative explanation, which we call "ignoring" has been overlooked by current theories of learning.  Our "ignoring" strategy can also be used to understand how our brains process information and make decisions, and it has important implications for our understanding of learning in general.

A particular mathematical structure, the root system of a Lie algebra, can be combined with a set of polynomials to form what are known as differential polynomials. Specifically, for the $E_8$ root system and a chosen rank, we examine certain polynomials. When the rank is 4 or 5, these differential polynomials create a Lie algebra that is isomorphic to the Gelfand-Fuchs algebra. As we increase the rank above 5, this property no longer holds, revealing a fundamental algebraic distinction within certain Lie algebras, particularly between $E_7$ and $E_8$.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds nearby polygonal curves for a given query, under the continuous Fréchet distance metric, which considers the parameters t and eps. A notable concern is that several current solutions require substantial memory, potentially rendering them impractical for certain applications. In this research, we develop a more efficient data structure for the c-approximate near neighbor problem with parametric segments, achieving a favorable trade-off between query time, preprocessing time, and memory usage. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of a data structure with certain performance characteristics for finding nearby curves, with a query time of O((c/eps)^4 log^2 n + (c/eps)^2 log (c/eps) + k) and a data structure size of O((c/eps)^2 (c log n + (c/eps)^2) n + (c/eps)^2 (c/eps)^2) for supporting parameter transformations, along with a more efficient data structure variant.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors in near-term quantum computers, various techniques have been developed, including those that rely on noiseless amplification of states (SNA) and those that amplify measurement bases directly (SNB). We introduce a technique that combines these approaches (SNBB) to amplify both states and measurement bases simultaneously. Under certain conditions, specifically when state preparation errors are negligible, our method outperforms existing techniques in correcting measurement errors. We also extend this approach to amplify both states and measurement sequences (SNBB'), which can amplify up to $k$ measurement sequences in addition to states. When $k$ is a large number, specifically $k\gg 1$, our method approaches the performance of previous techniques that amplify measurement sequences. We experimentally demonstrate the efficacy of our method on IBM's quantum hardware, specifically the 16-qubit IBMQ_Montreal quantum processor.

When humans control robots, they impose their own movements on the robot's actions. As a result, users often find it difficult to predict how their movements will affect the robot's behavior. To solve this, we've developed an adaptive learning system that allows a robot to adjust its behavior based on the user's movements. This system uses the robot's sensors to predict the user's intended movement and adjusts its behavior accordingly. To test this system, we've designed an experiment where a user controls a robot arm to pick up objects, and we've shown that the system successfully adapts to the user's movement.

For mobile robots to successfully interact with unknown environments, mapping algorithms are crucial components. Current mapping algorithms, however, are often too resource-intensive and difficult to adapt to changing environments. To address this issue, a novel algorithm has been developed that utilizes a combination of two techniques: a method to efficiently represent complex geometric structures and a technique to accurately estimate a robot's position within its surroundings. By integrating these methods with a framework that prioritizes processing speed, the new algorithm enables a robot to rapidly explore and build maps of unfamiliar environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing mapping algorithms in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Research into two-dimensional arrays has gained momentum due to potential applications in the research community. In wireless communication, arrays like patch and dipole antennas are being explored for use in multiple input multiple output systems and phased arrays, among other areas. This study investigates two-dimensional arrays further by generating a comprehensive database of array factor power patterns using a comprehensive approach. A range of two-dimensional arrays, including rectangular, harmonic, cubic, penta arrays, and arbitrary shapes, are analyzed and visualized. The resulting database is presented in two formats - a standalone application and a web-based platform - to facilitate easy access and manipulation. The application and website provide users with various tools to visualize, compare, and analyze array factor power patterns in multiple formats, while a built-in search feature allows for rapid identification of suitable arrays based on specific criteria. The dataset is further supplemented with two-dimensional pattern data, and the research findings are documented in a paper titled "A Comprehensive Database of Two-Dimensional Arrays: Applications, Visualization, and Search Functionality."

In this study, we examine the consequences of using a broad-spectrum X-ray source in a four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) system, particularly in terms of image quality. Our analysis reveals that when using such a source, distinct artifacts known as beam hardening, gradient, and diffusion artifacts can emerge. These distortions can manifest as contour shifts, density discrepancies, and blurred images, ultimately compromising image clarity. To address these issues, we have developed an iterative reconstruction technique that effectively corrects for beam hardening effects. Our proposed algorithm, which incorporates multiple corrections, demonstrates improved accuracy and reduced noise compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving a broad-spectrum X-ray source.

We investigate the validity of using a local response model to study light propagation in the nanoscale plasmonic structures. Our focus is on regions of intense electromagnetic field confinement, particularly within metallic areas, where we have found that the local field diverges as the wavelength approaches zero. This divergence is attributed to a non-physical exchange interaction that is not accounted for in the local quantum treatment. To address this issue, we have developed a nanoscale quantum model and incorporated it into a classical electromagnetic solver to solve the linear system of equations resulting from the combined models. Our results show that a more accurate boundary condition can be derived from the quantum model, which can be used to truncate the domain in the classical solver. Moreover, we have found that a quantum correction based on this boundary condition can be used to accurately account for the nonlocal effects in the classical simulations. Our approach has been successfully applied to a nanoscale waveguide and a nanoaperture, and we have found that it can lead to significant improvements in the accuracy of the simulations.

In this research, we examine the user's ability to locate contextually significant terms in a query and assess whether users can effectively utilize this knowledge in a retrieval task. We also compare human abilities with automated systems that automatically identify contextually significant terms. We conducted two studies, revealing that users can accurately identify terms with understanding, and often perform better than automated methods on both single and multi-term queries. However, we also found instances where automated term identification outperformed users and the necessity to balance human and machine abilities in information retrieval systems.

In various fields, multivariate time series data is becoming increasingly significant, and it is becoming essential to grasp its underlying patterns and trends. These patterns encompass aspects such as interconnected variables, intricate relationships between them, and the presence of external influences. To address this challenge, we have developed a new method called Zebra, which is a novel framework for automatically detecting and visualizing significant features in multivariate time series data. Zebra's design is rooted in expert knowledge, incorporates a series of analytical steps, and utilizes a series of visual outputs to provide a comprehensive understanding of the data. We have tested Zebra's effectiveness through our evaluation of a range of synthetic and real-world multivariate time series datasets, and the results demonstrate its ability to uncover previously unknown data characteristics.

Machine learning models can identify patterns within Electronic Health Records, suggesting new treatment and medication combinations to enhance healthcare and safety, a key public health goal. However, the data in these records is unstructured and diverse, with varying levels of detail and errors, which can hinder effective data mining. Our research focuses on developing a machine learning-based system that can automatically extract structured data from medical notes, enabling the generation of reliable evidence-based treatment and medication recommendations. A crucial aspect of this system is its ability to adapt to various medical domains and handle different types of data variability. To achieve this, we have developed a novel multi-task learning model that can simultaneously perform several related tasks, which helps the model to learn more efficiently and effectively. Our approach was tested on the MedNLI dataset, and the results show that our model can learn more efficiently, with up to 30% fewer parameters, while also achieving more accurate results, with up to 10% better performance. Furthermore, the performance of our model is not affected by the variability in the data, a common issue in the medical domain. Our multi-task learning model is a key component in the decision support system that suggests treatment and medication combinations based on medical records, a system that aims to improve healthcare and safety.

Using a mean-field approach, we study the behavior of an electrolyte near a charged surface that is influenced by the solvent's properties. We develop Poisson-Boltzmann equations to describe how the electrostatic potential is affected by surface charges and the surrounding electrolyte. These equations are discrete grid representations that can be efficiently solved and are equivalent to a cell-averaged, mean-field version of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations. Numerical simulations using a finite element method reveal that surface roughness can lead to significant differences in the electrolyte's behavior, which in turn affects the electrostatic potential and ion distributions.

Automating the labor-intensive process of extracting requirements from textual documents is a promising area of research. This study aims to leverage deep learning-based natural language processing techniques to address this challenge. A novel requirement identification system, named ReID, has been developed and tested on a large corpus of documents. By comparing it to a baseline model using the same input data, ReID achieved superior performance on both textual and image-based datasets across a range of metrics.

In this research, we examine the energy efficiency of a max-min optimization problem in a wireless network coding (WNC) system. We introduce a new model, maximum diversity network coding (MDNC), which allows for simultaneous communication between multiple pairs of nodes over a single WNC session. A mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) problem is formulated to maximize the minimum data rate among all nodes under a set of combined power and power allocation constraints. A linear programming formulation is then proposed to solve this problem and an efficient algorithm is developed to find a near-optimal solution. Simulation results demonstrate that MDNC can improve energy efficiency by a factor of 2.5 compared to scenarios without WNC. A comparison with prior work also reveals that MDNC can achieve a 15% gain in minimum minimum data rate while maintaining similar sum power levels.

A comprehensive theoretical study of YSR states in various systems has been conducted using a generalized Anderson model that accounts for the complex electronic structure of materials near Fermi level, as well as for systems with non-uniform hybridization with conduction electrons. This research showcases these aspects through simulations of a magnetic impurity on a d-wave superconductor and an analysis of YSR states in V and NbSe2 superconductors. Furthermore, the effects of non-equilibrium conditions and local heating on YSR states in both s- and d-wave superconductors have been explored.

A 90% confidence level sensitivity of one event has been achieved by the NA62 experiment for the rare kaon decay process K+ to pi+ plus two neutrinos. The experiment analyzed an enormous dataset of 10^17 positive kaons, utilizing a highly sensitive detector system, and was able to apply stringent cuts that minimized background to less than 0.001 events. As a result, the data collected is consistent with the predictions of the standard model, and includes sensitivity ranges of 1.2 to 16 GeV/c for momentum, and 0.15 to 0.9 GeV/c^2 for mass, allowing the NA62 results to set the most precise upper limits on this decay process to date.

We introduce a novel approach to aligning point clouds from moving objects by utilizing their 3D geometric and visual cues. Traditional methods that rely solely on geometry struggle with high noise levels and dynamic elements, while our proposed technique achieves accurate registration even in areas with little structural detail. By combining visual information, point clouds can be precisely aligned, overcoming limitations imposed by dynamic elements and geometric distortions. Experimental evaluations demonstrate our approach outperforms existing methods in registering vehicle scans, particularly in complex and demanding environments.

Satellite imagery is widely used across multiple sectors, encompassing fields such as weather forecasting, ocean monitoring, urban planning, and more. The process of collecting and analyzing satellite data is typically automated, relying on the analysis of vast amounts of collected images. Although numerous algorithms have been developed to analyze this data, they often require human intervention to adjust parameters or manual oversight. To minimize the need for human involvement, we've developed an open-source deep learning-based algorithm that automatically classifies satellite images into discrete levels. This algorithm, known as OASIS, was initially trained using a combination of public and private datasets, comprising a total of 106 billion pixels. The OASIS model was then applied to a publicly available dataset, where it outperformed existing algorithms by achieving higher overall accuracy, F1 scores, and Kappa coefficients. Furthermore, we've established a public repository to facilitate the transferability of the OASIS model to new environments.

In X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES), the effects of an intense X-ray beam can lead to significant modifications in the spectrum, particularly at high photon fluxes. We have developed a theoretical framework to describe these non-linear effects and applied it to L$_{2,3}$-XANES of Fe$^{2+}$. Our model considers two primary factors contributing to the observed changes: valence electron excitation and the presence of core holes, which can form either spontaneously or through resonant Auger processes. Our calculations align well with experimental data from Fe$^{2+}$, and through deconvolution, we have isolated individual contributions from each factor. Furthermore, our model can be used to analyze the electronic state changes in Fe$^{2+}$ induced by an intense X-ray beam, which are found to depend on the excitation of valence electrons, the presence of core holes, and the excitation of plasmons. These changes can also be influenced by the excitation of other electrons, such as L$_{2,3}$, and by energy transfer to other electronic systems, which may lead to changes in the local temperature and excitation of other electrons.

In wireless communication, a technique known as automatic modulation classification is crucial for ensuring reliable, secure transmission. It's essential for detecting and identifying unknown signals in cognitive radio and military applications. This study provides an overview of recent advancements in automatic modulation classification, focusing on deep neural networks and their effectiveness even in challenging environments. We discuss the performance of Deep Neural Networks in classifying various modulation schemes, including high-order and complex modulations, across different scenarios. Additionally, we highlight the research challenges and propose potential future directions in this field.

Segmenting MS lesions in MRI images is an essential yet complex task, hindered by the loss of detailed information in conventional deep learning approaches, particularly when using 3D U-Net. Our proposed approach, L*Net, tackles this limitation by incorporating detailed features from 2D and 3D feature maps. L*Net's multi-branch architecture processes these 2D maps individually, while a separate branch analyzes the 3D map. The combined results from these branches enable a more accurate and detailed segmentation. Our experiments on two public datasets demonstrate L*Net's superior performance, with the DMT MRI dataset showing a DSC of 0.7920 and a Dice Distance of 0.1440, and the MultiMS dataset revealing a DSC of 0.7322 and Dice Distance of 0.1888. L*Net's improved DSC is 0.0490 and 0.0190 compared to 3D U-Net on the respective datasets.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, under the assumption that the manifold adheres 
to the MP condition as introduced by C. Wang and X. Wang.

In the context of ergodic continuous-time systems, we explore the trade-off between model complexity and generalization. Utilizing tools from differential equations, we establish a key theorem that sets a limit on a system's generalization error in relation to its model complexity and a key parameter, T. When T is set to a specific value, we can derive a specific type of differential equation, and we show that this system has the simplest possible structure, and it has the best possible generalization ability. We also demonstrate that this system has a specific invariant behavior, and it can be used to model a key parameter, $\lambda$, in a system. We further investigate the relationship between this system and a key parameter, $\lambda$, in a system, and we show that this system has the best possible generalization ability. Finally, we show that this system has the simplest possible structure, and it can be used to model a key parameter, $\lambda$, in a system.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores within the Lynd-Bird 257 (LCM-257) infrared dark cloud, a small and compact source in the Taurus-Auriga molecular cloud complex, has been conducted. The cloud was observed using the VLA and the ATCA at a wavelength of 3.2 mm. The resulting data set comprised 110 cores with sub-arcsecond resolution. The distribution of these cores spans a mass range of approximately 0.04 to 1.8 solar masses. The research found that the cores in the cloud can be divided into two distinct groups: protostellar and quiescent. The former group, consisting of six cores, has masses greater than 0.5 solar masses, while the latter group, consisting of 104 cores, has masses less than 0.5 solar masse. The analysis also found that the cores are concentrated in the central 10 arcseconds of the cloud. The research found that the cloud's mass is approximately 1.5 solar masses. The theory of primordial black holes (PBHs) suggests they represent a form of black hole. It has been proposed that PBH mass distributions could be clustered, prompting an examination of how gravitational lensing affects this distribution. Our analysis reveals that a single image can misleadingly distort the perceived PBH mass spectrum, creating apparent features such as peaks and valleys. However, accounting for multiple images in a statistical manner preserves the underlying smoothness of the PBH mass spectrum.

We have conducted extensive research using Monte Carlo simulations to analyze the phase transitions of monodisperse molecules with asymmetric shapes. By simulating the system using a lattice model, we observed that molecules with shapes resembling convex polygons can exhibit liquid crystalline phases, including nematic and smectic A states, even at low packing densities. Notably, our study revealed that these shape-induced phases disappear when the packing density falls below 0.5, except in cases where the molecules have a very high aspect ratio. Furthermore, we discovered that a particular type of molecule shape can give rise to an ordered hexagonal lattice at very low packing densities, resulting in a type of ordered state known as hexatic. Our research also revealed that this type of ordered state can be achieved with molecules shaped like equilateral triangles at a much lower packing density than in hard disk systems.

Deep learning models have seen widespread adoption in various fields, but their growing complexity poses a challenge in terms of efficient adaptation to new tasks. To address this issue, we introduce Parameter-efficient tuning for TAnsfer Learning (PiTL), a novel approach for quickly transferring pre-trained models to new tasks with a substantial reduction in trainable parameters. PiTL achieves this through a hybrid architecture that combines the original model with a smaller adapter model, where only the adapter model's parameters are adjustable during training. This approach allows for a seamless integration of multiple adapter models across tasks and datasets, and demonstrates significant improvements in both efficiency and performance on a range of NLP benchmarks, including part-of-speech tagging, Named Entity Recognition, and Question Answering.

This paper examines a simple yet profound problem, where we aim to determine if two distinct collections of data points are equivalent after an additional element is introduced to both. Using an in-depth case study on basic one-dimensional datasets, we investigate the capabilities and limitations of the homomorphism neural network architecture in this context. By applying a specific network design that compares two sets based on the count of elements within defined intervals, we identify the types of functions that can be effectively utilized to solve this problem. The results reveal that some functions can successfully detect when the sets are already symmetric, making further comparisons unnecessary, while other functions can only recognize when the sets are completely identical.

This study provides theoretical foundations for applying thermodynamic principles to polymer fluids and other complex substances. By employing entropy and enthalpy, we can describe the energetic states of these systems, while internal energy and pressure determine entropy, mirroring gas behavior. Although similar equations describe configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy of polymer fluids and liquids, distinct principles govern their behavior. Our results for free volume and entropy are applicable to liquids, glasses, and complex substances.

Transformer-based language models are increasingly being used for logical reasoning tasks, but they struggle with using negative statements, according to our investigation. We developed a set of challenges designed to test the limitations of first-order logic, which we found causes a significant increase in the complexity of the text being generated. Furthermore, we created the Woodwork problem, which demonstrates how transformer models are prone to making errors when combining information from separate sentences, resulting in a notable decline in their ability to accurately understand negative statements. We also identified a gap in existing datasets, which fails to adequately assess the ability of these language models to use negative statements, leading us to propose a new challenge called the Glass problem. This challenge highlights the importance of maintaining context when a language model encounters a negative statement, especially when combined with complex sentence structures. We propose the Locust problem, which showcases how these language models struggle to maintain consistency in their understanding of entities across multiple sentences. We found that all challenges related to negative statements reveal a significant weakness in transformer models' ability to reason logically, with their performance dropping significantly when faced with these challenges.

In neural machine translation, the attention mechanism allows each generated word to be influenced by all preceding words via a context vector. However, since we don't fully understand how attention relates to the memory of RNNs, we've investigated this connection. Our research reveals that the attention mechanism essentially functions as a method of retrieving relevant information from the memory. We've discovered that the similarity between generated words' one-dimensional projections and all preceding words' projections serves as our calculated attention values. We've also found that the attention mechanism's effectiveness is contingent on the dimensionality of these projections. We've further demonstrated that the similarity metric's sensitivity to the projection's dimensions plays a crucial role in determining the effectiveness of our attention mechanism.

This passage provides a brief overview of the techniques employed in our research, specifically the methods used to establish a symplectic filling of the connected sum of two Genus-2 symplectic surfaces, as well as its implications for the Witten-Yang-Mills theory. 

To express the weights of curvature graphs in the homology of the surfaces, we will use a generalization of the Birman-Wenzl algebra of tangles, which allows us to derive any weight in the homology $H_*(\Sigma_{g;1})$ from a set generated by a specific set of curvature graphs on the surface $\Sigma_g$. 

We will build upon previous work done by the first author and D. Sugiyama, which utilized a simplified version of this algebra in the context of Surface Homeomorphism Problems. Furthermore, our research reveals an intriguing finding: any homology class in the mentioned homology space can be expressed using only the homology classes derived from the specified generating set of curvature graphs.

This work builds on the findings of \cite{Hartman:2013cta} by examining the large N limit of entanglement entropy in arbitrary odd dimensions. We utilize holographic duals of odd dimensional BTZ black holes and apply counterterm methods to compute the entropy. Our results show that the vacuum entanglement entropy on S^{d-2} in the large N limit grows exponentially with N, consistent with a general conjecture. Additionally, using the Euclidean approach, we derive the first two corrections to this results in the large N limit.

Carr and Li's 2008 algorithm is a numerical method used to value Asian options based on Markov processes. This algorithm is initially applied to a one-dimensional process and can be extended using the dimension mixing approach to work with higher-dimensional Markov processes and options that involve multiple assets. This paper presents a numerical approach for valuing options on asset averages in a multi-dimensional setting. It also includes results using the Moler M-file and convergence analysis for the Matheron method, which is implemented in MATLAB.

The origin of gamma-rays in the sky remains a significant mystery, yet it's evident that some galactic and extragalactic sources do not account for all gamma-rays, leaving some unresolved. This could be due to the limitations of current gamma-ray telescopes in identifying specific emitters. This work focuses on the diffuse gamma-ray background, considering various types of astrophysical objects that could be the emitters. These include supernovae remnants, pulsar wind nebulae, supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, microquasars, and active galactic nuclei. By utilizing data from the Fermi Large Telescope and other multi-messenger observations, researchers have derived models to explain gamma-ray emission from galactic and extragalactic origins. This involves analyzing gamma-ray spectra, energy spectra, and luminosity functions. The resulting models are then used to simulate gamma-ray emission from various astrophysical objects and assess their potential contributions to the gamma-ray background. The findings indicate that certain types of sources, such as supernovae and gamma-ray bursts, could be the primary contributors to gamma-ray emission. However, precise identification of these emitters requires future observations at higher energies and energies beyond 100 TeV.

This article explores the connection between the behavior of classical fluctuations during an inflationary period and the emergence of classical gravity as a more localized quantum state. We examine how these fluctuations in the early universe can be mathematically described using the path integral method, which is widely used in physics. A proposed time-dependent equation is introduced to make solving for classical gravity in the early universe more feasible. We also discuss the significance of this approach in the context of an expanding universe.

The need for interpretable visual models is significant, yet developing such models remains a challenge. This difficulty stems from a lack of a standardized approach to improve model interpretability. This research introduces a novel framework called CoViNeT, a sophisticated convolutional neural network with multiple layers that can accurately classify images while also providing clear explanations for its predictions. By employing attention mechanisms, the network highlights key areas in input images that contribute to its classification, making its decision-making process easier to understand. This approach was successfully tested on various image datasets, including those with different levels of complexity, and demonstrated its ability to focus on the most relevant image regions. Additionally, the network was found to be resilient against common image manipulations, such as noise addition, cropping, and other transformations, making it a reliable choice for real-world applications.

In cuprate materials, long-range electron-phonon coupling plays a significant role, influencing various phenomena. A model that considers the effect of localized bosons on electrons and their interactions is examined. A mathematical analysis of a two-dimensional model that incorporates these interactions demonstrates the existence and properties of its ground state. Furthermore, the properties of the model are studied in relation to localized bosons and electron parameters. A surprising result of this investigation is that even weak coupling, when combined with a large value of a specific parameter, can lead to the emergence of a non-Fermi liquid state, contrary to conventional expectations.

This research investigates the causal connections between social risk factors and HIV prevalence in six African nations. Causal relationships are quantified using information-theoretic dependencies, which can be directly derived from n-dimensional probability distributions without the need for parametric models. The analysis reveals that female education and HIV awareness are interrelated in DRC, Namibia, and South Africa. Conversely, male education and HIV awareness show significant correlation in Botswana, Ghana, and South Africa. Furthermore, our findings suggest that marriage rates influence HIV prevalence in DRC, Ghana, and South Africa, while children under five are associated with HIV in Namibia, Botswana, and South Africa. The study's results provide a novel perspective on the causal factors contributing to the HIV epidemic in these countries.

In a three-dimensional chiral magnet with a nearest-neighbor Heisenberg exchange interaction and a weak magnetic anisotropy, we investigate the behavior at low temperatures using a variational Monte Carlo method. This approach enables us to study the ground state of the system in detail. Our findings reveal that the system exhibits a complex phase diagram with various states, including a uniform state with a magnetization aligned along one of the lattice directions, localized states with a magnetization aligned along another direction, and Skyrme lattice phases with either a triangular or pyrochlore skyrmon lattice structure. Moreover, we discovered that the lowest energy state of the system is a topological Skyrme lattice rather than a uniform state.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are versatile statistical tools,
applicable to a broad range of time series data, and have significant
potential in finance applications. Despite their benefits, a unified review
of their theoretical underpinnings and practical uses is currently missing.
This article fills this void, offering a comprehensive examination of the
key aspects of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models. The paper begins by
outlining the historical context and fundamental concepts before delving into
critical issues such as model identification, parameter estimation, model
evaluation, forecasting, and forecasting innovation. Additionally, the
article explores relevant software tools and highlights several
applications in the field of finance.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline of the most effective strategy for resolving these special cases of the equilibrium problem, utilizing the best-known solution approaches like best response, gradient, and proximal gradient methods.

This paper explores a more nuanced understanding of predictive models by employing probabilistic methods, which can be achieved through techniques like Bayesian deep learning. We examine the predictive uncertainty in Deep Gaussian Process models, a type of fully probabilistic model, and find that it captures the distinct forms of uncertainty inherent in data. By analyzing the posterior distribution of these models, we observe the presence of both epistemic and data noise uncertainties, which can be distinguished from one another. We also identify the uncertainty associated with the numerical optimization used to approximate the model posterior and develop methods to quantify this uncertainty, which we refer to as "optimization uncertainty." We propose "deep uncertainty," a novel metric that integrates epistemic, data noise, and optimization uncertainties to provide a comprehensive measure of the predictive uncertainty in these models. We demonstrate the utility of this notion in real-world datasets and explore the relationship between the different uncertainty forms, revealing that each can be represented as a sum of Gaussian and non-Gaussian components.

The effectiveness of Taylor's diffusion theorem in calculating turbulent transport coefficients from dynamo simulation results is assessed. Specifically, we examine the accuracy of these coefficients in a model of dynamo action in an elliptical cylinder under axial twist. We also evaluate the applicability of these coefficients to different geometries, such as a spherical shell with and without an external magnetic field.

A study of the fastest molecular gas outflow in the galaxy NGC4945 has been conducted using the ALMA telescope. Observations revealed a molecular gas outflow in the east-northeast direction, with a velocity of approximately 200 km/s relative to the galaxy's systemic velocity. This outflow, centered around a 60 pc wide region near the galaxy's nucleus, features a 200 pc wide gas plume that extends up to 1 degree from the nucleus in a nearly straight line. The outflow's properties were examined through a model of a jet-driven wind, and it was found that the wind's mass outflow rate is estimated at around 0.1-0.3 solar masses per year, driven by nuclear activity rather than star formation. This discovery of the fastest gas outflow in a star-forming galaxy to date suggests that active galactic nuclei can have a significant impact on the galaxy's star formation process, with potential feedback effects that could alter the galaxy's evolution.

A simplified model has been developed to describe the 3-magnetosonic-resonance in magnetized plasmas without considering pressure or finite-temperature effects. This basic model is similar to the original one introduced by Chen in 1990. However, it omits the influence of ion cyclotron resonance. Consequently, it can be analytically simplified into a cubic equation. Furthermore, this model is applicable to both cold and warm ion scenarios. A graphical analysis is provided to illustrate the resonance conditions for different scenarios. In addition, a numerical simulation has been conducted to investigate the growth rate and damping frequency associated with this resonance phenomenon.

Previous studies on second derivative methods have primarily focused on constant step size approaches for solving ODEs. This research extends second derivative general linear methods with variable step sizes, allowing for more efficient solving of ODEs and DAEs. To accomplish this, specific formulas for numerical approximation and linear stability are developed, alongside theoretical proofs for existence and rationality. Furthermore, numerical examples and practical tests validate the proposed methods, demonstrating their efficiency in solving ODEs and DAEs.

We establish a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of the Lyapunov inequality A*X + Y + Q = 0 in a Hilbert space. Specifically, if there's a positive, self-adjoint, bounded solution (Qi in the positive self-adjoint ones) to the inequality, then the generator A has a spectrum strictly in the left half-plane. This implies a key result that even if the Hilbert space is infinite dimensional, the growth of T is still bounded by the distance of the spectrum from the imaginary axis, which is a new finding.

A unique method for creating dimuonium atoms has been explored by directing a 5 GeV muon beam through a thin carbon foil. The interaction between muon-muon and the foil's nuclei results in the formation of dimuonium. The behavior of dimuonium as it passes through matter is characterized by its characteristic length, defined as the average distance a dimuonium atom travels before breaking apart. The breaking apart process is influenced by the presence of the muon beam, and its effect on the behavior of dimuonium is observed by comparing dimuonium produced with and without the muon beam. The presence of the muon beam is found to have a significant effect on the motion of dimuonium, and its effect is observed by measuring the energy loss of dimuonium in the presence and absence of the muon beam. The energy loss of dimuonium is compared to the energy loss of muon mu anti-muon anti-muon and muon anti-muon pairs, and the agreement between the measured energy loss and the expected energy loss is found to be good.

Portfolio managers assess their performance in relation to market standards, such as the Standard & Poor 500 index.  A key issue is often reported when managers fail to achieve benchmark parities like mean, median, or 80th percentile.  To address this problem, a novel approach is proposed that views portfolio performance as a distribution and uses a transformation method to align it with benchmark performance.  This approach is based on a two-stage process: first, the cumulative distribution function of portfolio returns is estimated, and then a quantile transformation is applied to generate adjusted returns.  A simulation of this method demonstrates its effectiveness in achieving benchmark parities and maintains key return characteristics like bias and efficiency.  Additionally, the proposed method is compared to traditional risk adjustment techniques like adjusting for market risk using beta or mean-correcting returns, showing it as a comprehensive tool for evaluating performance relative to a benchmark.

The most prevalent galaxy type, dwarf galaxies, exhibit the smallest, least complex, and least understood interstellar mediums (ISMs). This study aims to investigate the diverse ISMs of these galaxies. We utilized a collection of 129 JWST/MIRI spectra, previously obtained as part of the ISM Exploration of the Local Universe project, to analyze the ISMs of 11 dwarf galaxies. By employing a novel approach, we successfully detected atomic and ionic species in 11 out of 12 galaxies, including carbon monoxide, atomic hydrogen, and helium. Our findings show that carbon monoxide is present in 11 galaxies, with carbon and hydrogen abundances varying significantly, suggesting the presence of distinct ISM phases. This study uniquely identifies the 100 micron fine structure line in 8 out of 11 galaxies, providing the first detection of this line in galaxies with low metallicity. Our results reveal that galaxies with low metallicity tend to have ISMs lacking in molecular material, in contrast to their more metal-rich counterparts. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the ISMs of 11 dwarf galaxies, including their atomic and molecular species, and highlights the distinct ISM phases present in these galaxies.

We analyze the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson system where the quasiparticles interact with the background bosons. The fermions move through the boson background, generating fermionic quasiparticles that also emit and absorb bosons. The quasiparticles' stability is analyzed in the context of the quasiparticle self-energy, where a pole in the self-energy's Fourier-transformed retarded Green's function indicates quasiparticle stability. The system is examined in the non-relativistic regime, where the dispersion relation is linear, and the interaction potential is arbitrary. The stability condition is derived in terms of the phase space volume occupied by the quasiparticle and its surrounding bosons. The pole's position in the complex plane is determined in terms of the quasiparticle energy, Planck constant, and phase space volume. The findings are also applicable to a relativistic scenario, where the dispersion relation is relativistic, and the stability condition is expressed in terms of the relativistic gamma factor. The study provides insights into the behavior of fermionic quasiparticles in various contexts, including the electron in a plasma and the Weyl fermion in a photon gas.

Golan and Shalev extended Thompson's groups X, F, and T to more general algebraic structures using words, graphs, and trees, with the original groups being specific instances. In doing so, they explored how these new groups relate to classical results on the growth and divergence of finite groups. In this context, the non-abelian free group serves as a specific case. In our research, the generalization to words, graphs, and trees is shown to yield rapid divergence in the Thompson's-like groups, with the exception of certain special scenarios. The only notable exceptions are tree-like subgroups of $V_n$ that are analogous to the classical Thompson's groups.

The original Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture is a popular system for question answering that combines text retrieval and natural language generation. However, our analysis reveals that the original design has a significant drawback: it requires manually setting a threshold to filter out irrelevant retrieval results. To address this limitation, we propose a fully automated, end-to-end RAG architecture that eliminates the need for such hyperparameter tuning. Our system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets, including SQuAD, SciFact, and MedQA, by outperforming the conventional RAG architecture with a significant margin.

This study introduces recurrence relations and first-kind differential equations for 
orthogonal polynomials in a class with a parameter, all under a logarithmic weight.

The advent of crowdsourcing platforms has made it possible to rapidly gather
annotations from a large number of contributors. Nevertheless, these
contributors' expertise, motivation, and reliability vary, which can
significantly impact the quality of the annotations produced. To
address this issue, a new statistical model has been developed that
considerably improves annotation quality by taking into account the
individual contributors' influence. This model, known as LCFM, is a
latent factor model that utilizes both the annotations and the
corresponding contributors' information to estimate the underlying data
representation and the contributors' position within this representation.
By using an iterative process to estimate the annotations and the
contributors' quality, along with a new optimization algorithm called
ALADIN, accurate results can be obtained. Experiments conducted on real
datasets demonstrate that ALADIN outperforms existing methods,
significantly increasing the accuracy of annotations.

We introduce TS2-Net, a novel deep learning model for single image super-resolution, specifically targeting images captured by multi-pixel color filters. Our approach employs a multi-scale shift-transformer architecture to capture spatial correlations among pixels affected by color filters. This is achieved through the dynamic rearrangement of pixel positions, which enhances the representation of spatial features. Subsequently, our local feature extraction module transforms these features into a localized representation, which is then transformed into a high-resolution grayscale image using the convolutional multi-spectral rearrangement module. Through comprehensive evaluations on public datasets, it is demonstrated that TS2-Net outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in single image super-resolution tasks.

We've identified new signs of flavour-changing neutral currents in the top quircle sector, which can be explored through theoretical models featuring right-handed leptophilic scalars and a non-standard weak interaction. Our research suggests that these currents can be influenced by the mixing of a top quark and a flavourless scalar, and this effect is primarily constrained by two main factors: the rate at which top quarks decay and a proposed relationship between certain Yukawa couplings. Despite these limitations, we found that we can still explore a wide range of possible values for a flavour-changer coupling, particularly in scenarios involving right-handed charged leptons. Our analysis reveals that we can search for flavour-changing signals by examining the rate at which Higgs bosons decay into pairs of charged leptons, and this can be done by studying existing data from the Large Hadron Collider and planning future runs.

In this study, we examine a network model that integrates rules from preferential attachment and uniform attachment. Starting with an initial single edge, we sequentially add new vertices, each time forming a new link between an existing vertex and the new one. A new approach, preferential uniform attachment, is proposed where the likelihood of selecting an existing vertex is determined by the sum of its degree and a uniform random value. As a result, our model exhibits properties of both preferred and uniform connections. Through theoretical analysis, we investigate the degree distribution of the generated networks and demonstrate that it adheres to a discrete Weibull distribution. Furthermore, we investigate the limiting degree distribution and show that it converges to an exponential distribution under certain conditions. Moreover, we numerically examine our model's degree distribution and degree fluctuation, finding that it has a smaller variation compared to the preferential attachment model.

This research presents a new deep convolutional neural network-based algorithm for interference cancellation across a broad range of signal types. We initially develop a model that formulates interference cancellation as a regression problem, allowing it to be applied to complex signals like 5G and software-defined radio, as well as simpler radio signals. Our proposed model outperforms existing linear and non-linear interference cancellation techniques in both linearly and non-linearly separable interference scenarios, achieving superior cancellation levels.

This article provides an overview of the effects of gravitational influence on quantum systems. Beginning with a general discussion of Gravitational Fields (GFs), the text then delves into the specifics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics in the presence of a GF. It follows with an examination of Gravitational Interactions, the impact of black holes on quantum states and the theory of quantum gravity.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood by analyzing the particle flux across any plane in a proton. Generalized parton distributions (GPDs) can be obtained by examining specific types of processes, such as a proton scattering off an electron, where we study different combinations of kinematic variables. We can also obtain other GPDs by studying various processes, such as a proton scattering off a neutron, where we study different combinations of kinematic variables. We have proposed a new process, involving the study of a proton scattering off a neutron, where we study different combinations of kinematic variables, that can be used to obtain a wide range of GPDs.

AI systems frequently make mistakes, but their errors differ from those made by humans due to their unique nature. This study delves into how incorporating bias mitigation can reduce mistakes in AI models, using a multi-task learning framework for text classification. A comparison is made between the impact of a model that corrects for errors and one that doesn't, revealing that models that account for errors tend to make fewer mistakes. Furthermore, the same model applied to different tasks shows a correlation between the number of errors and task difficulty, indicating that as errors decrease, the difficulty increases.
